title: 3-Read Friday #90: Vocabulary Instruction, AI and Neuromyths, and Boring Teaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #90 spans vocabulary pedagogy, AI reliability, and teaching philosophy. Jake Cowling translates Engelmann's Theory of Instruction into a plain, teachable sequence for explicitly teaching words with precision. Korbinian Moeller and Markus Spitzer then share research finding that ChatGPT and similar models are good at catching educational neuromyths when asked directly, but far worse at catching them when the myths are embedded implicitly in ordinary teaching questions. SoL in the Wild closes the issue with a defence of deliberately "boring" teaching, arguing that visible engagement and durable learning are often at odds. Barton flags Book 8 of his Tips for Teachers series, on Diagnostic Questions.
points: Cowling's piece is framed by Barton as a successful translation of dense Engelmann and Carnine theory into "plain, teachable moves," praised for the quality of the result rather than just the ambition.

The Moeller/Spitzer research finding is the issue's most immediately actionable AI-literacy takeaway: models catch neuromyths well when asked directly, but far worse when a myth is embedded implicitly in a realistic teaching question.
SoL in the Wild's "boring teacher" piece provides the issue's philosophical closer, arguing that visible classroom energy and durable long-term learning are frequently in tension rather than aligned.

Across the three picks, Barton's issue traces a line from precise instructional design (Cowling), to AI's reliability limits (Moeller/Spitzer), to a broader argument about what teaching should actually look like day to day (SoL in the Wild).
quotes: Jake’s aim for this post is to translate the core principles of Englemann’s Theory of Instruction into plain, teachable moves when explicitly teaching words. The results are excellent.

This fascinating study finds that models such as Chat GPT outperform humans at identifying educational neuromyths (such as we only use 10% of our brain) when asked directly, but falter when such myths are implicitly included in everyday teaching questions.
A positive reflection on why being a boring teacher can actually mean being a really effective teacher.
